chapters.title: Part I: Accounting for Partnership: Basic Concepts

topics.title: Nature of partnership

learn.hook: Two college friends in Pune start a cloud-kitchen and split the profit 50:50. Without signing anything formal, they may already be partners in the eyes of the law!
points: Section 4 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 defines partnership as the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all.
Essential features: two or more persons, an agreement (oral or written), a lawful business, sharing of profits, and mutual agency (each partner is both an agent and a principal).
Liability of partners is unlimited: if the firm's assets fall short, partners' private assets can be used to pay the firm's debts. Partners are jointly and severally liable.
Minimum 2 partners; the maximum is 50 under the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014.
Accounts special to partnership: partners' capital (and current) accounts, the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account, and adjustments when the firm is reconstituted.

example.q: Meera and Kabir jointly inherit a flat in Jaipur and share the rent they get from it. Are they partners?
steps: Check each feature: two persons – yes; sharing of returns – yes.
But there is no agreement to carry on a business; they merely co-own property.
Sharing income from jointly owned property does not by itself create a partnership.
example.answer: No. Co-owners sharing rent are not partners, because there is no agreement to carry on a business together.

learn.reallife: Many Indian CA firms, law chambers and family-run kirana wholesalers in Chandni Chowk work as partnership firms because partnership is quick to form and needs no heavy legal process.

quiz.q: Which section of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 defines 'partnership'?
quiz.explain: Section 4 gives the definition. Section 13 covers rights such as interest on loans, and Section 48 deals with settlement on dissolution.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the definition section with other well-known sections of the Act

quiz.q: What is the maximum number of partners a partnership firm can have under the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014?
quiz.explain: Rule 10 of the 2014 Rules prescribes a maximum of 50 partners.
quiz.mistake: Remembers the older limits of 10/20 or the Companies Act upper ceiling of 100

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an essential feature of a partnership?
options: Sharing of profits of a business
quiz.explain: Registration is optional under the Act. Agreement, business, profit sharing and mutual agency are essential.
quiz.mistake: Thinks registration is a condition for a partnership to exist

quiz.q: 'Mutual agency' in a partnership means that:
options: each partner must contribute equal capital
the firm is an agent of its customers
only the senior partner can bind the firm
each partner is an agent of the firm and of the other partners, and also a principal
quiz.explain: Every partner can bind the firm by acts done in the ordinary course of business and is, in turn, bound by the acts of others.
quiz.mistake: Confuses mutual agency with equal capital or with a single managing partner

quiz.q: A firm's assets are ₹6,00,000 and its outside liabilities are ₹9,00,000. What happens to the shortfall?
options: Partners must pay it from their private assets, as their liability is unlimited
Only the partner with the highest capital pays it
The firm is converted into a company
quiz.explain: Partners are jointly and severally liable without limit, so creditors can recover the ₹3,00,000 shortfall from partners' personal assets.
quiz.mistake: Treats a partnership like a company with limited liability

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Two people who jointly own a godown and share its rent are not partners.
Reason (R): A partnership arises only from an agreement to carry on a business and share its profits.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Co-owning property and sharing its rent is not carrying on a business by agreement, which is exactly what R states.
quiz.mistake: Assumes any sharing of income creates a partnership

quiz.q: Which pair of accounts is special to partnership firms and not needed by a sole proprietor?
options: Partners' current accounts and the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
quiz.explain: A sole trader takes the whole profit, so there is no appropriation among owners. Partners need appropriation and separate capital/current accounts.
quiz.mistake: Lists general accounting records common to all businesses

quiz.q: Which minimum number of persons is needed to form a partnership?
quiz.explain: Partnership is a relation between persons, so at least two are needed. Seven is the minimum for a public company.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up partnership with the minimum membership of a public company

teach.ask: Gappu thinks any two people who share money are partners. Explain the essential features of a partnership.
teach.praise: Perfect! Agreement, business, profit sharing and mutual agency – now Gappu knows a partnership when he sees one.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: is it just sharing money, or must there be an agreement to run a business with each partner acting as agent?

topics.title: Partnership deed and rules when there is no deed

learn.hook: Friends fall out over money more often than over cricket. A partnership deed is the rulebook that prevents the fight before it begins.
points: A partnership deed is the written agreement among partners, ideally stamped as per the Indian Stamp Act. It usually states the firm's name, capital of each partner, profit-sharing ratio, interest on capital and drawings, salary/commission, rules for admission, retirement and dissolution, and how accounts are kept.
If there is no deed (or the deed is silent), the Act applies: profits and losses are shared equally.
No deed: no interest on capital, no interest on drawings, and no salary or commission to any partner.
No deed: a partner's loan to the firm earns interest at 6% p.a. (Section 13).
Interest on a partner's loan is a charge against profit, debited to the Profit and Loss Account, so it is allowed even if the firm makes a loss. It is not an appropriation.

example.q: Asha and Vikram have no deed. Asha's capital is ₹5,00,000 and Vikram's ₹3,00,000. Vikram also lent the firm ₹1,00,000 on 1 April 2025. Profit for 2025-26 before any interest is ₹86,000. Divide the profit.
steps: No deed → no interest on capital; partners share equally.
Vikram's loan gets 6% p.a.: ₹1,00,000 × 6% = ₹6,000, charged to the Profit and Loss Account.
example.answer: Interest on loan to Vikram ₹6,000; profit share ₹40,000 each.

learn.reallife: Many CA firms, clinics and family businesses in Bengaluru run as partnership firms, and the partners' first legal document is the deed that spells out who gets what.

options: No, a partner gets no salary unless the deed or partners' agreement provides it
Yes, but only at half the rate
Only if the firm earns more than ₹5,00,000
quiz.explain: Without a deed, no partner is entitled to salary or commission, however much time is devoted.
quiz.mistake: Thinks extra effort automatically earns remuneration

quiz.q: Rohan's capital is ₹4,00,000 and Simran's is ₹2,00,000. There is no deed. The firm's profit is ₹90,000 and there are no loans. Simran's share of profit is:
quiz.explain: With no deed, profit is shared equally regardless of capital: ₹90,000 ÷ 2 = ₹45,000.
quiz.mistake: Shares profit in the capital ratio 2:1

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Interest on a partner's loan is paid even if the firm suffers a loss.
Reason (R): Interest on a partner's loan is a charge against profit.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
quiz.explain: Because it is a charge (an expense), it must be paid whether there is profit or loss.
quiz.mistake: Treats loan interest like interest on capital, which needs profits

quiz.q: Which of these does a partnership deed usually NOT contain?
options: Rate of interest on capital and drawings
Rules for admission and retirement of partners
The personal income-tax return of each partner
quiz.explain: A deed records the terms of the partnership among partners, not their personal tax filings.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the deed records all personal finances of partners

teach.ask: Gappu's firm has no deed. Tell him what the law says about sharing profit, interest and salary.
teach.praise: Spot on! Equal sharing, no interest on capital or drawings, no salary, and 6% on loans – Gappu has the rulebook.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: what rate does a partner earn on a loan given to the firm when there is no deed?

topics.title: Fixed and fluctuating capital accounts

learn.hook: Two accounts or one? The choice decides whether a partner's capital looks rock-steady like Mount Abu or bobs up and down like a boat on the Ganga.
points: Fixed capital method: each partner has a Capital Account and a Current Account. The capital account changes only when capital is added or permanently withdrawn.
Under the fixed method, interest on capital, salary, commission, share of profit, drawings and interest on drawings go to the Current Account.
Fluctuating capital method: only one Capital Account per partner; all these adjustments are recorded in it, so its balance keeps changing.
A fixed capital account always shows a credit balance; a current account (or a fluctuating capital account) can show a debit balance.
If the question does not say which method to use, prepare fluctuating capital accounts.

example.q: Under fixed capitals, Nisha's capital is ₹5,00,000 and her current account opens with ₹20,000 Cr. During the year: interest on capital ₹50,000, salary ₹30,000, profit share ₹60,000, drawings ₹40,000, interest on drawings ₹2,000. Find her closing balances.

learn.reallife: Big Indian partnership firms like audit firms often fix each partner's capital and run a current account, so the stake stays clear while yearly earnings flow separately.

quiz.explain: Heavy drawings or losses can make the current account debit, while the fixed capital account stays credit.

It is not shown at all
quiz.explain: A debit balance means the partner owes money to the firm, so it is an asset of the firm.

Assertion (A): Under the fixed capital method, a partner's drawings are debited to the current account.
Reason (R): Under this method, the capital account changes only when capital is introduced or withdrawn permanently.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Since the capital account is kept fixed, regular drawings must go elsewhere – the current account.
quiz.mistake: Fails to link why the current account exists

quiz.q: Fixed capital method: Meena's capital is ₹4,00,000; her current account opens at ₹10,000 Dr. During the year she gets interest on capital ₹32,000 and a profit share of ₹48,000; her drawings are ₹50,000. Her closing current account balance (credit) is:
quiz.explain: Start at −10,000, add 32,000 and 48,000, subtract 50,000: the result is +20,000, a credit balance.
quiz.mistake: Treats the opening debit balance as a credit

teach.ask: Gappu cannot tell fixed capital from fluctuating capital. Explain the difference.
teach.praise: Great! Fixed = capital plus current account; fluctuating = one capital account that takes every adjustment.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: under the fixed method, where do drawings and profit share go?

topics.title: Profit and Loss Appropriation Account

learn.hook: The firm has made its profit. Now comes the IPL-auction moment – who gets what, in which order?
points: The Profit and Loss Appropriation Account is an extension of the Profit and Loss Account. It starts with net profit and shows how it is distributed among partners.
Debit side: interest on capital, salary/commission to partners, transfer to reserve, and finally each partner's share of profit. Credit side: net profit (b/d) and interest on drawings.
Commission as a % of net profit before charging it = NP × rate/100. After charging it = NP × rate/(100 + rate).
Transfer to reserve is an appropriation; the remaining profit is then divided in the profit-sharing ratio.
Entry for appropriation items: Dr Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c, Cr Partners' Capital (or Current) A/cs; for interest on drawings: Dr Partners' Capital/Current A/cs, Cr P&L Appropriation A/c.

example.q: Net profit ₹4,00,000. Interest on capital: A ₹30,000, B ₹20,000. Salary to B ₹50,000. Interest on drawings: A ₹4,000, B ₹6,000. Transfer to reserve ₹40,000. A and B share 3:2. Find each share of profit.

learn.reallife: A family-run sweets firm in Kolkata may pay the partner who runs the shop floor a salary first, put some profit aside as reserve before Durga Puja, and share the rest.

topics.title: Interest on capital

learn.hook: Money parked in a fixed deposit earns interest. Money parked in your firm deserves a reward too – if the deed says so.
points: Interest on capital is allowed only if the deed provides it. It is calculated on the opening capital for the year.
Additional capital introduced during the year earns interest from the date of introduction; capital withdrawn stops earning interest from the date of withdrawal.
Unless the deed treats it as a charge, interest on capital is an appropriation, so it is allowed only out of profits. If the firm makes a loss, no interest on capital is allowed.
If the profit is less than the total interest on capital, the available profit is divided in the ratio of interest on capital of each partner.
Working back: Opening capital = Closing capital − profit share credited − additional capital + drawings + losses debited (before interest on capital).

example.q: Anil's capital on 1 April 2025 is ₹4,00,000. He adds ₹1,00,000 on 1 October 2025. Interest on capital is 10% p.a. Find interest for the year ending 31 March 2026.

learn.reallife: An RBI repo-rate change ripples into FD rates, and firms often link the interest-on-capital rate in their deed to such market rates.

quiz.explain: Reverse the year: remove the profit share and the additional capital, and add back the drawings.

quiz.q: X's capital is ₹6,00,000 and Y's ₹4,00,000. Interest on capital is 5% p.a. Profit is ₹75,000, shared equally after interest. X's total (interest + share):
quiz.explain: X's interest ₹30,000; Y's ₹20,000. Balance ₹25,000 shared equally, so X gets ₹12,500 more.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add the interest to X's profit share

quiz.q: When the profit is less than the total interest on capital (interest payable only out of profit), the profit is divided in the ratio of:
options: capitals at the end of the year
interest on capital due to each partner
quiz.explain: The available profit is shared in proportion to the interest each partner would have received.
quiz.mistake: Uses the profit-sharing ratio by habit

quiz.q: Interest on capital is normally calculated on:
options: closing capital for the full year
opening capital, adjusted for capital added or withdrawn on a time basis
quiz.explain: Closing capital already includes the year's profit; interest is on capital actually used during the year.
quiz.mistake: Uses closing capital, which already includes the current year's profit

teach.ask: Gappu wants to calculate interest on capital. Tell him the rules.
teach.praise: Super! Opening capital, time basis for changes, nothing in a loss, and the ratio of interest when profits fall short.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: what if the profit is smaller than the total interest on capital?

topics.title: Interest on drawings

learn.hook: Taking money out of the firm for your sister's wedding shopping? The firm may charge you interest – and the date you withdraw matters.
points: Interest on drawings is charged only if the deed provides it. It is calculated for the time the money stays out of the business, up to the end of the year.
Different amounts on different dates: use the product method – multiply each amount by the months remaining, add the products, then interest = total products × rate/100 × 1/12.
Equal monthly drawings for a full year: average period 6.5 months (beginning of each month), 6 months (middle) and 5.5 months (end).
Equal quarterly drawings for a full year: average period 7.5 months (beginning of each quarter), 6 months (middle) and 4.5 months (end).
Dates not given: charge for 6 months on the total. If a flat rate is given (not 'per annum'), time is ignored.

example.q: Partner Leela withdrew ₹10,000 on 1 July, ₹20,000 on 1 October and ₹15,000 on 1 January. The year ends on 31 March; interest is 6% p.a. Find interest on drawings.

learn.reallife: Just as a bank charges interest from the day a credit-card amount is spent, a firm charges interest on drawings from the day money is withdrawn.

topics.title: Guarantee of profit to a partner

learn.hook: A star player joins a team only if promised a minimum fee. Firms do the same for a key partner – a guaranteed minimum profit.
points: A guarantee of profit assures a partner a minimum amount of profit. If his actual share is less, the shortfall (deficiency) is made good by the other partner(s).
Guarantee by the firm: the deficiency is borne by all the other partners in their profit-sharing ratio.
Guarantee by a particular partner: that partner alone bears the deficiency.
Guarantee by some partners in an agreed ratio: the deficiency is borne in that agreed ratio.
If the partner's actual share is equal to or more than the guaranteed amount, no adjustment is needed.

example.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C is guaranteed ₹60,000 by the firm. Profit is ₹3,00,000. Distribute it.
steps: A and B bear it 3:2: A ₹6,000, B ₹4,000.

learn.reallife: Start-ups that bring in an experienced CFO as a partner often promise a minimum yearly profit share to attract them, just as franchises guarantee fees to star cricketers.

topics.title: Past adjustments

learn.hook: Accounts closed, profits shared – and then someone notices interest on capital was forgotten. Do we reopen everything? No – one smart entry fixes it.
points: Past adjustments are needed when items such as interest on capital, interest on drawings or salary were omitted or wrongly given after the accounts were closed, or profit was shared in a wrong ratio.
Prepare a statement: (1) credit what each partner should have got, (2) debit what should have been charged, (3) reverse the wrong profit share and redistribute it correctly, (4) find the net effect.
The net effects add up to zero, because the firm's total profit does not change.
Pass one adjusting entry: Dr the partner(s) with net excess received / Cr the partner(s) with net shortfall. With fixed capitals, use current accounts.
For a wrong ratio, the net effect is simply (correct share − share actually given) for each partner.

example.q: A and B have capitals of ₹3,00,000 and ₹1,00,000. Profit of ₹80,000 was shared equally, but interest on capital at 10% p.a. was omitted. Pass the adjusting entry.
steps: This ₹40,000 should have reduced profit shared equally: debit each ₹20,000.
example.answer: Dr B's Capital A/c ₹10,000 / Cr A's Capital A/c ₹10,000

learn.reallife: Just as Indian Railways issues a refund instead of re-running a train, accountants fix past errors with a single correcting entry instead of redoing the year's accounts.

quiz.mistake: Expects the omitted amount to appear as a net figure

quiz.explain: With fixed capitals, all such adjustments go through current accounts.

chapters.title: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Admission of a Partner

topics.title: Reconstitution and admission of a partner

learn.hook: A new bowler joins the team mid-season. The team continues, but the dressing-room agreement changes. That is reconstitution of a firm.
points: Reconstitution: any change in the existing agreement among partners while the firm continues – a change in profit-sharing ratio, admission of a partner, retirement or death of a partner, or amalgamation of two firms.
A new partner acquires two main rights: a share in the assets of the firm and a share in its future profits.
The new partner usually brings capital (for his share of assets) and a premium for goodwill (to compensate old partners for the profit share they give up).
Adjustments on admission: new profit-sharing ratio and sacrificing ratio, goodwill, revaluation of assets and liabilities, accumulated profits/reserves and losses, and partners' capitals.

example.q: Neha and Sameer run a design studio. They admit Tara as a partner. List the accounting issues they must settle.
steps: Decide Tara's share and work out the new ratio and the sacrificing ratio.
Value goodwill and record Tara's premium for goodwill.
Revalue assets and liabilities; distribute reserves and accumulated profits/losses to Neha and Sameer.
Record Tara's capital and adjust the capitals if required.
example.answer: New and sacrificing ratios, goodwill, revaluation, reserves and accumulated profits/losses, and capital adjustment.

learn.reallife: When a growing Indian start-up brings in a new co-founder, lawyers redraft the agreement and accountants revalue assets – the same steps as admitting a partner.

options: Conversion of the firm's cash into bank deposits

quiz.explain: When two firms amalgamate, a new agreement among partners arises – a reconstitution.

topics.title: New profit-sharing ratio and sacrificing ratio

learn.hook: Like slicing a pizza for a late-arriving friend: someone gives up a slice. The maths tells you exactly whose plate shrinks and by how much.
points: New share of an old partner = old share − share given up (sacrificed) to the new partner.
If nothing is said about sacrifice, old partners sacrifice in their old ratio; then the sacrificing ratio = old ratio.
If old partners surrender a fraction OF THEIR OWN share, sacrifice = old share × that fraction.
Sacrificing ratio = old share − new share, for each old partner. It is used to distribute the new partner's premium for goodwill.
Always check: the new shares of all partners must add up to 1.

example.q: A and B share 3:2. C is admitted for 1/5 share, taken from A and B in their old ratio. Find the new ratio.
steps: Remaining share for A and B = 1 − 1/5 = 4/5.

learn.reallife: IPL franchises re-split ownership stakes when a new investor joins, exactly the way partners work out a new ratio.

topics.title: Goodwill: meaning, factors and need for valuation

learn.hook: Why do people queue outside a famous chaat stall in Lucknow when a new one across the road is empty? That pull is goodwill.
points: Goodwill is the value of a firm's reputation that lets it earn more than normal profits. It is an intangible asset – it has value but no physical form – and is not a fictitious asset.

Factors raising goodwill: favourable location, efficient management, favourable market situation (monopoly or limited competition), nature of business (stable demand), special advantages such as licences, patents, trademarks and long-term contracts.
Goodwill must be valued when there is a change in profit-sharing ratio, admission, retirement or death of a partner, dissolution involving sale of the business, or amalgamation of firms.
Goodwill cannot be sold separately; it goes with the business.

example.q: A sweet shop opposite a busy railway station earns ₹2,00,000 a year while similar shops earn ₹1,40,000. What explains the gap?
steps: Same product, same capital – the difference is the extra footfall from the location.
That ability to earn ₹60,000 more than normal is what goodwill represents.
example.answer: A favourable location gives the shop goodwill – the capacity to earn above-normal profit.

learn.reallife: Brands like Amul built goodwill over decades through quality and trust; a new partner joining such a business pays for a slice of that pull.

topics.title: Valuing goodwill: average and weighted average profit

learn.hook: A firm earned ₹80k, ₹1 lakh and ₹1.2 lakh over three years. How much is its reputation worth today? Two quick methods give the answer.
points: Average profit method: Goodwill = Average profit × Number of years' purchase.
Average profit = total of (normal) past profits ÷ number of years. A loss year is subtracted, not added.
Weighted average method: multiply each year's profit by a weight (usually 1, 2, 3… with the latest year highest), add the products, divide by the total of weights. Use it when profits show a trend.

Normalise profits before averaging: deduct abnormal gains (e.g. profit on sale of a fixed asset), add back abnormal losses (e.g. loss by fire), and deduct any reasonable remuneration of a partner not charged.

example.q: Profits for three years: ₹60,000, ₹90,000 and ₹1,20,000 (latest). Value goodwill at 2 years' purchase of weighted average profit with weights 1, 2, 3.

learn.reallife: Analysts valuing an Indian listed company also clean up profits for one-time items, like a one-off land sale, before applying a multiple – just like normalising profits.

quiz.explain: Total = 5,00,000 (loss subtracted); average 1,25,000; × 3 = ₹3,75,000.
quiz.mistake: Adds the loss as if it were a profit

quiz.mistake: Takes the simple average (₹90,000) instead of the weighted one

quiz.q: Profits: ₹1,10,000; ₹1,40,000 (includes ₹20,000 profit on sale of land); ₹1,20,000 (after a ₹10,000 loss by fire). Goodwill at 2 years' purchase of normal average profit:
quiz.mistake: Leaves abnormal items in the profits

quiz.q: Average profit is ₹1,50,000, but a working partner's reasonable salary of ₹30,000 a year has not been charged. Goodwill at 3 years' purchase:
The weighted average profit method is preferred when:
options: profits are the same every year
profits show a rising or falling trend
the firm has made losses in all years
quiz.explain: Weights give more importance to recent years, which better reflect the trend.
quiz.mistake: Thinks weighting is needed for stable profits

quiz.q: Goodwill valued at 2.5 years' purchase of average profit is ₹3,00,000. Average profit is:
quiz.explain: Average profit = Goodwill ÷ years' purchase = 3,00,000 ÷ 2.5.

quiz.explain: Abnormal gains will not recur, so they are removed before averaging.
quiz.mistake: Treats abnormal gains as normal income

teach.ask: Gappu must value goodwill from past profits. Explain the average and weighted average methods.
teach.praise: Superb! Clean the profits, average them (weighted if there's a trend) and multiply by years' purchase.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: what should he do with a one-time profit from selling land before averaging?

topics.title: Super profit and capitalisation methods

learn.hook: Every firm in the industry earns 10% on capital. Yours earns 16%. That extra 6% – the super profit – is the real engine of goodwill.
points: Normal profit = Capital employed × Normal rate of return ÷ 100. Capital employed = Total assets (excluding goodwill and fictitious assets) − Outside liabilities.
Super profit = Average profit − Normal profit. Goodwill = Super profit × Number of years' purchase.
Capitalisation of average profit: Capitalised value = Average profit × 100 ÷ Normal rate; Goodwill = Capitalised value − Actual capital employed.
Capitalisation of super profit: Goodwill = Super profit × 100 ÷ Normal rate of return.
Both capitalisation methods give the same goodwill for the same data.

example.q: Capital employed ₹5,00,000; normal rate 10%; average profit ₹80,000. Find goodwill by (a) super profit at 3 years' purchase, (b) capitalisation of average profit.

learn.reallife: When a large Indian company acquires a profitable start-up, it pays far more than the net assets – the excess is goodwill, often justified by super profits.

quiz.q: Capital employed ₹5,00,000; normal rate 10%; average profit ₹80,000. Goodwill at 3 years' purchase of super profit:
quiz.explain: Normal profit ₹50,000; super profit ₹30,000; × 3 = ₹90,000.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies average profit instead of super profit

quiz.q: Average profit ₹80,000; normal rate 10%; capital employed ₹5,00,000. Goodwill by capitalisation of average profit:
quiz.explain: Capitalised value ₹8,00,000 less capital employed ₹5,00,000 = ₹3,00,000.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to deduct the actual capital employed

quiz.q: Super profit is ₹24,000 and the normal rate of return is 12%. Goodwill by capitalisation of super profit:
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by the rate instead of dividing

quiz.q: Total assets ₹7,00,000 (including goodwill ₹50,000); outside liabilities ₹1,50,000. Capital employed for valuing goodwill:
quiz.mistake: Includes goodwill already in the books

quiz.q: Capital employed ₹6,00,000; normal rate of return 15%. Normal profit:
'Super profit' means:
options: the highest profit in any past year
the excess of average profit over normal profit
average profit multiplied by years' purchase
quiz.explain: It is the extra profit the firm earns above what similar firms normally earn on the same capital.
quiz.mistake: Confuses super profit with the best year's profit

quiz.q: Goodwill by the super profit method at 2 years' purchase is ₹1,20,000. Normal profit is ₹1,00,000. Average profit is:
quiz.mistake: Adds goodwill directly to normal profit

quiz.q: Average profit ₹1,50,000; normal rate 12%; capital employed ₹10,00,000. Goodwill by capitalisation of average profit:

teach.ask: Gappu's firm earns more than normal. Explain super profit and the capitalisation methods.
teach.praise: Brilliant! Normal profit from capital employed, super profit as the excess, and capitalisation by 100 ÷ normal rate.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: how does he find the normal profit before working out super profit?

topics.title: Premium for goodwill brought in cash or kind

learn.hook: The newcomer pays for a seat at the table. Who pockets that payment – and why no 'Goodwill Account' shows up?
points: AS 26: goodwill is recorded only when purchased for consideration. So on admission no Goodwill Account is raised; the new partner's premium is used instead.
Premium brought in cash: Dr Cash/Bank A/c, Cr Premium for Goodwill A/c; then Dr Premium for Goodwill A/c, Cr Sacrificing Partners' Capital A/cs (in sacrificing ratio).
If old partners withdraw the premium: Dr their Capital A/cs, Cr Cash/Bank A/c. If retained, no further entry.
Premium in kind: Dr the asset brought (e.g. Machinery), Cr Premium for Goodwill A/c and the new partner's Capital A/c.
Premium partly brought: the unpaid part is debited to the new partner's Capital (or Current) A/c and credited to sacrificing partners.

example.q: A and B share 3:2. C joins for 1/5 share. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,50,000 and C brings his premium in cash. Pass the entries.
steps: Sacrifice in old ratio 3:2: A ₹18,000, B ₹12,000.
Dr Bank 30,000 / Cr Premium for Goodwill 30,000.
Dr Premium for Goodwill 30,000 / Cr A's Capital 18,000, Cr B's Capital 12,000.

learn.reallife: Think of the 'entry fee' a new partner pays in a big Mumbai CA firm: it goes straight to the partners whose profit share shrinks.

Under AS 26, goodwill is recorded only when it is ___.

quiz.explain: Only purchased goodwill can be recorded, so the premium mechanism is used.
quiz.mistake: Raises self-generated goodwill in the books

quiz.explain: C's premium ₹30,000 shared 3:2 → A ₹18,000.

quiz.explain: C's premium = 30,000; sacrificing ratio 2:1; A gets 2/3 = ₹20,000.

Dr sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs / Cr Premium for Goodwill A/c
Dr Cash A/c / Cr all partners' Capital A/cs in new ratio

quiz.mistake: Reverses the entry or raises a goodwill account

options: Dr old partners' Capital A/cs / Cr Cash A/c
Dr Cash A/c / Cr old partners' Capital A/cs
Dr Premium for Goodwill A/c / Cr Cash A/c
quiz.explain: Withdrawal reduces their capital and the firm's cash.

quiz.q: C brings machinery worth ₹1,00,000: ₹70,000 as capital and ₹30,000 as premium for goodwill. The entry is:
options: Dr Machinery ₹1,00,000 / Cr C's Capital ₹70,000, Cr Premium for Goodwill ₹30,000
Dr Goodwill ₹30,000, Dr Machinery ₹70,000 / Cr C's Capital ₹1,00,000
quiz.explain: The asset is debited; the amount is split between his capital and the premium.
quiz.mistake: Credits the whole asset to capital, ignoring the premium

quiz.q: C should bring ₹30,000 as premium but brings only ₹18,000. Amount debited to C's Capital/Current A/c:
quiz.explain: The part not brought (30,000 − 18,000) is debited to his account and credited to sacrificing partners.
quiz.mistake: Debits the amount brought instead of the shortfall

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Premium for goodwill brought by a new partner is credited to old partners in their sacrificing ratio.
Reason (R): Old partners give up a part of their future profits to the new partner.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Compensation follows sacrifice, so R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the premium with the sacrifice

teach.ask: Gappu's new partner brought cash for goodwill. Explain where it goes.
teach.praise: Perfect! The premium goes to the sacrificing partners' capitals – and no Goodwill Account is raised under AS 26.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: which partners get the premium, and in what ratio?

topics.title: Goodwill not brought, existing goodwill and hidden goodwill

learn.hook: Sometimes the newcomer cannot pay for goodwill, sometimes old goodwill sits in the books, and sometimes goodwill hides inside the capital he brings. Let's catch all three.
points: New partner unable to bring premium: Dr New Partner's Capital (or Current) A/c, Cr Sacrificing Partners' Capital A/cs (sacrificing ratio).
Goodwill already in the books: write it off among OLD partners in the OLD ratio – Dr Old Partners' Capital A/cs, Cr Goodwill A/c.
Hidden goodwill = Total capital of the new firm (implied by the new partner's capital and share) − (Old partners' adjusted capitals + New partner's capital).
Hidden goodwill is not shown in books; the new partner's share of it is treated as his premium for goodwill.

example.q: A and B have adjusted capitals of ₹1,00,000 and ₹80,000. C brings ₹80,000 for 1/4 share. Find hidden goodwill and C's share of it.
steps: C's share = 60,000 × 1/4 = ₹15,000, debited to C and credited to A and B in sacrificing ratio.

learn.reallife: A rookie investor putting ₹80 lakh into a firm for a 1/4 stake when the books show much less is signalling the hidden goodwill the market sees.

His share of goodwill is adjusted through his account.
Existing goodwill in the books is written off among all partners, including the new one, in the new ratio.
It is written off among old partners in the old ratio.
Hidden goodwill is recorded in a Goodwill Account.
It is inferred; the new partner's share is adjusted like premium.
Hidden goodwill arises when the new partner's capital implies a larger total capital than the actual total.
That gap is goodwill.
With fixed capitals, unpaid premium is debited to the new partner's current account.
Fixed capital accounts are not disturbed.

Dr Goodwill A/c / Cr D's Capital A/c
Dr sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs / Cr D's Capital A/c
quiz.explain: D is charged for his share of goodwill and the sacrificing partners are compensated.
quiz.mistake: Raises a goodwill account or reverses the entry

quiz.explain: Existing goodwill is written off among old partners in the old ratio: 40,000 × 3/5.
quiz.mistake: Uses the new ratio or writes it off equally

quiz.explain: Implied total ₹3,20,000 less actual ₹2,60,000 (including C's capital) = ₹60,000.
quiz.mistake: Leaves C's own capital out of the actual total

quiz.explain: Sacrificing ratio 1:1, so B gets half of ₹24,000.
quiz.mistake: Uses the old ratio instead of the sacrificing ratio

quiz.q: Why is existing goodwill written off when a new partner is admitted?
options: Because goodwill becomes worthless on admission
Because goodwill is adjusted through the new partner's premium, and the old goodwill belongs to the old partners
Because the new partner demands it
Because goodwill is a current asset
quiz.explain: Writing it off in the old ratio clears the books so goodwill is adjusted only through premium, as AS 26 requires.
quiz.mistake: Thinks goodwill has lost its value

quiz.q: Hidden goodwill arises when:
options: the new partner brings more cash than the old partners
the capital implied by the new partner's contribution exceeds the actual combined capital of all partners
the firm has a debit balance in the Profit and Loss Account
quiz.explain: The gap between implied and actual capital is attributed to goodwill.
quiz.mistake: Compares only the new partner's capital with old partners'

quiz.q: Capitals are fixed. The new partner's unpaid share of goodwill is debited to his:
quiz.explain: Fixed capitals stay unchanged; adjustments go to the current account.

teach.ask: Gappu's new partner can't pay for goodwill, and there is old goodwill in the books. Explain what to do.
teach.praise: Great job! Charge the newcomer's account, write off old goodwill in the old ratio, and spot hidden goodwill from capitals.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: in what ratio is goodwill already in the books written off?

topics.title: Accumulated profits, losses and reserves on admission

learn.hook: Before a new player joins, the old team splits the savings in the kitty. Reserves belong to the people who earned them.
points: General reserve, credit balance of Profit and Loss and similar accumulated profits: Dr Reserve/P&L A/c, Cr Old Partners' Capital A/cs (old ratio).
Accumulated losses and deferred revenue expenditure (debit balance of P&L, Advertisement Suspense): Dr Old Partners' Capital A/cs, Cr P&L/Advertisement Suspense A/c (old ratio).
Workmen Compensation Reserve: first meet the claim; any excess goes to old partners in old ratio. If the claim exceeds the reserve, the excess claim is debited to Revaluation A/c.

Investment Fluctuation Reserve (NCERT also calls it Investment Fluctuation Fund): first absorb the fall in market value of investments; the balance goes to old partners. If the fall exceeds the reserve, the extra is debited to Revaluation A/c.
Alternatively, reserves may be left undisturbed: the new partner's capital is debited with his share, and sacrificing partners are credited, by a single entry.

example.q: Workmen Compensation Reserve is ₹30,000 and the claim is ₹20,000. A and B share 3:2. Show the treatment.
steps: Cr Provision for Workmen Compensation Claim 20,000.
Cr A's Capital 6,000 and B's Capital 4,000 (excess 10,000 in 3:2).
example.answer: Claim ₹20,000 provided; excess ₹10,000 shared A ₹6,000, B ₹4,000.

learn.reallife: Factories in Gujarat keep workmen compensation reserves for accident claims; when partners change, the unused part goes to those who built it up.

quiz.explain: The claim is provided for first; the excess ₹10,000 goes to old partners.

quiz.mistake: Debits the full fall to revaluation

quiz.q: Partners decide not to disturb a General Reserve of ₹60,000. C is admitted for 1/4 share. Amount debited to C's Capital in the adjusting entry:
quiz.explain: C would get 1/4 of the reserve in future, so he compensates sacrificing partners now: 60,000 × 1/4.
quiz.mistake: Charges C with the entire reserve

quiz.q: Why are accumulated reserves distributed among old partners in the old ratio on admission?
options: Because the new partner refuses them
Because reserves are liabilities to outsiders
They were earned when the old partners shared profits in that ratio
quiz.explain: Past profits belong to those who shared them, in the ratio then in force.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the new partner has a right to past profits

teach.ask: Gappu's firm has a general reserve and some advertisement suspense when a new partner joins. Explain the treatment.
teach.praise: Well done! Reserves credited and fictitious losses debited to old partners, both in the old ratio.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: in which ratio, and to whom, does the general reserve go?

topics.title: Revaluation of assets and reassessment of liabilities

learn.hook: That office in Gurugram bought years ago is worth much more now. Before a new partner joins, the old partners should pocket that gain.
points: Revaluation Account (a nominal account) records changes in asset and liability values on reconstitution.
Credit: increase in assets, decrease in liabilities, unrecorded assets. Debit: decrease in assets, increase in liabilities, unrecorded liabilities.
Balance: profit (credit side larger) or loss, transferred to OLD partners' capital accounts in the OLD ratio.
Entry for increase in asset: Dr Asset A/c, Cr Revaluation A/c. Decrease: Dr Revaluation A/c, Cr Asset A/c. Profit: Dr Revaluation A/c, Cr Old Partners' Capital A/cs.
After revaluation, prepare partners' capital accounts and the new balance sheet with revised values.

example.q: A and B (3:2) admit C. Building ₹2,00,000 is increased by 20%; stock ₹60,000 reduced by 10%; a 5% provision is made on debtors of ₹50,000; unrecorded investments ₹7,000; unrecorded outstanding salary ₹3,500; creditors reduced by ₹2,000. Find the revaluation result.

learn.reallife: Land prices along new metro lines in Delhi, Bengaluru and Pune have jumped, so firms owning property there often show big revaluation gains when partners change.

old partners in their old ratio

quiz.explain: All reconstitution gains are credited to A's capital account, and its closing balance goes to the new balance sheet: 2,00,000 + 22,200 + 30,000.

teach.ask: Gappu must revalue his firm's assets before a new partner joins. Explain the Revaluation Account.
teach.praise: Excellent! Gains on the credit side, losses on the debit side, and the result goes to old partners in the old ratio.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: who gets the revaluation profit – and in which ratio?

topics.title: Adjustment of partners' capitals on admission

learn.hook: After all adjustments, do the partners' capitals match their profit shares? If not, someone tops up and someone withdraws.
points: Case 1 – new partner's capital from old partners' capitals: Total capital of new firm = Combined adjusted capitals of old partners ÷ their combined new share; New partner's capital = Total × his share.
Case 2 – old partners' capitals from new partner's capital: Total capital = New partner's capital ÷ his share; each old partner's required capital = Total × his new share.
Adjusted capital = capital after goodwill, reserves, revaluation and similar adjustments.
Excess capital is withdrawn (Dr Capital, Cr Cash) or transferred to current account; deficiency is brought in cash (Dr Cash, Cr Capital) or debited to current account.

example.q: C is admitted for 1/4 share and brings ₹60,000. New ratio A:B:C = 2:1:1. A's adjusted capital is ₹1,30,000 and B's ₹50,000. Adjust capitals.

learn.reallife: Like co-founders topping up their stake before a funding round, partners align capital with their new profit shares.

topics.title: Change in profit-sharing ratio among existing partners

learn.hook: No one joins or leaves, yet the shares change – perhaps one partner now works harder. Whoever gains must pay the one who gives up.
points: On a change in ratio, some partners gain and some sacrifice: gain = new share − old share; sacrifice = old share − new share.
Goodwill: the gaining partner compensates the sacrificing partner for his share of goodwill – Dr Gaining Partner's Capital A/c, Cr Sacrificing Partner's Capital A/c.
Reserves and accumulated profits/losses are distributed in the OLD ratio (or adjusted by a single entry between gaining and sacrificing partners).
Revaluation profit or loss on a change in ratio is shared in the OLD ratio.

chapters.title: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Retirement/Death of a Partner

topics.title: Amount due to a retiring or deceased partner

learn.hook: A senior partner of a Chennai textile firm retires after 25 years. What exactly should his cheque say? Let's build the figure line by line.
points: Amount due = credit balance of capital (and current) account, plus his share of goodwill, reserves and accumulated profits, revaluation profit, profit up to the date of retirement/death, interest on capital and any salary/commission due.

Deduct: drawings, interest on drawings, his share of revaluation loss, accumulated losses (debit balance of P&L) and fictitious items (e.g. advertisement suspense), and any debit balance of his current account.
All these adjustments are posted to his capital account; its final balance is the amount payable.
The same rules apply on death; the amount is then payable to the deceased partner's executors.

example.q: C retires. Capital ₹1,00,000; share of goodwill ₹30,000; share of reserve ₹12,000; revaluation profit share ₹6,000; profit till retirement ₹8,000; interest on capital ₹2,000; drawings ₹15,000; interest on drawings ₹500. Amount due?

learn.reallife: Just as a retiring government employee receives a final settlement that adds gratuity and leave encashment and subtracts dues, a retiring partner's dues are added and subtracted item by item.

quiz.explain: Revaluation profit belongs to all old partners, including the retiring one.

quiz.explain: Accumulated losses are borne by all partners in the old ratio, including the retiring one.

Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

quiz.mistake: Thinks interest on drawings is earned by the partner

quiz.q: The final amount payable to a retiring partner is:
options: his capital plus the firm's total reserve
the balance of his capital account after all adjustments
his share of the firm's total assets at book value

quiz.explain: A debit balance in the current account reduces his dues: 80,000 + 20,000 − 5,000.

topics.title: New ratio and gaining ratio on retirement

learn.hook: When a partner leaves, his slice of the cake is shared by those who stay. How much extra does each one get?
points: New share of a continuing partner = old share + share acquired from the retiring partner.
If nothing is stated, continuing partners take the retiring partner's share in their old ratio, so the new ratio equals their old mutual ratio.
Gaining ratio = new share − old share, for each continuing partner.
Gaining ratio is used on retirement/death; sacrificing ratio (old − new) is used on admission.
If the new ratio is given, compute gains directly; a partner may gain nothing.

example.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires and A and B take his share equally. Find the new ratio and gaining ratio.

learn.reallife: When a senior doctor retires from a private clinic partnership in Hyderabad, the remaining doctors split his share – exactly the gaining-ratio calculation.

items.q: Retiring share 1/5 split equally. Each gains?
B old 2/5, takes 1/10 more. New share?
Retiring 3/10; A takes 2/3 of it. A gains?

items.text: Gaining ratio = new share − ___ share.
If not stated, continuing partners gain in their ___ ratio.
The retiring partner's goodwill is debited to continuing partners in the ___ ratio.

quiz.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires. Nothing is said about the new ratio. The new ratio of A and B is:
quiz.explain: When silent, continuing partners keep their old mutual ratio, 3:2.

quiz.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires and his share is taken equally by A and B. New ratio:
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add the acquired share to the old share

quiz.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires; A and B take his share in 2:1. New ratio:
quiz.mistake: Splits C's share in the old ratio instead of 2:1

options: Only A gains; B's share is unchanged
quiz.mistake: Assumes gaining ratio always equals the new ratio

quiz.explain: A's gain = new 3/5 − old 2/5 = 1/5.
quiz.mistake: Takes A's new share as his gain

quiz.q: Gaining ratio differs from sacrificing ratio because:
options: gaining ratio is used only on dissolution
gaining ratio is new share minus old share, used mainly on retirement/death; sacrificing ratio is old minus new, used mainly on admission
sacrificing ratio is calculated on capital
quiz.explain: They measure opposite movements and are used in different reconstitutions.

quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order or uses Z's share

teach.ask: Gappu's partner is retiring. Explain the gaining ratio and how the new ratio is found.
teach.praise: Fantastic! Gain = new share minus old share, and the new ratio adds the retiring share to the continuing partners.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: how is the gaining ratio different from the sacrificing ratio?

topics.title: Treatment of goodwill on retirement or death

learn.hook: The retiring partner helped build the firm's name. When he leaves, the partners who keep enjoying that name must pay him for it.
points: Under AS 26, no Goodwill Account is raised. The retiring/deceased partner's share of goodwill is credited to his capital and debited to continuing partners in the GAINING ratio.
Entry: Dr Continuing Partners' Capital A/cs (gaining ratio), Cr Retiring Partner's Capital A/c.
Goodwill already in the books is first written off among ALL partners (including the retiring one) in the OLD ratio.
Hidden goodwill: if the amount agreed to be paid exceeds his dues (before goodwill), the excess is his share of goodwill – debited to continuing partners in gaining ratio.

example.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires. Goodwill is valued at ₹1,20,000. Pass the entry.
steps: Gaining ratio (nothing stated) = old ratio of A and B = 3:2.
Dr A's Capital 12,000; Dr B's Capital 8,000 / Cr C's Capital 20,000.

learn.reallife: When a founding partner of a well-known Indian law firm retires, the remaining partners effectively buy his share of the firm's reputation.

Goodwill is charged only to gainers.
Hidden goodwill on retirement is the excess of the amount paid over the dues before goodwill.

Dr Goodwill A/c / Cr all partners' Capital A/cs (old ratio)

Dr Cash A/c / Cr Goodwill A/c

quiz.explain: C's share ₹20,000 is borne by A and B in 3:2 → A ₹12,000.
quiz.mistake: Debits A with his own share of the whole goodwill

quiz.explain: Existing goodwill is written off by ALL partners in the old ratio: 60,000 × 1/6.
quiz.mistake: Leaves the retiring partner out of the write-off

quiz.explain: The extra ₹20,000 paid is his share of goodwill.
quiz.mistake: Treats the full payment as goodwill

quiz.explain: Only A gains (1/5); C's share (1/5 × 1,00,000 = ₹20,000) is fully debited to A.
quiz.mistake: Splits it in the new ratio 3:2

options: Because the retiring partner chooses that ratio
The continuing partners gain his share of future profits in that ratio
Because the firm's capital is in that ratio

quiz.explain: Those who gain must compensate in proportion to their gain.
quiz.mistake: Uses the new ratio by habit

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A Goodwill Account is not raised when a partner retires.

options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

quiz.explain: B's share = 90,000 × 2/6 = ₹30,000 (debited to A and C ₹15,000 each).
quiz.mistake: Credits B with only one gainer's debit

teach.ask: Gappu's partner retires. Explain how goodwill is handled under AS 26.
teach.praise: Excellent! Continuing partners are debited in the gaining ratio and the retiring partner credited – no goodwill account.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: which partners are debited for the retiring partner's goodwill, and in which ratio?

topics.title: Revaluation and reserves on retirement or death

learn.hook: The retiring partner should not lose out if the factory is now worth more, nor escape if the stock has lost value.
points: Assets and liabilities are revalued on retirement/death, and unrecorded assets and liabilities are brought into the books.
Revaluation profit or loss is shared by ALL partners, including the retiring/deceased partner, in the OLD ratio.
Reserves and accumulated profits (General Reserve, P&L credit balance) are credited to all partners in the old ratio.
Accumulated losses and fictitious assets (P&L debit balance, advertisement suspense) are debited to all partners in the old ratio.

example.q: A, B and C share 2:2:1. C retires. Building is increased by ₹25,000; stock reduced by ₹5,000; an unrecorded liability of ₹5,000 is recorded. General reserve is ₹50,000. Find C's share of each.

learn.reallife: A retiring partner of a Kochi spice-export firm benefits if the warehouse near the port has appreciated – revaluation captures that gain before he leaves.

An unrecorded liability is credited to the Revaluation Account.

continuing partners in the gaining ratio

quiz.explain: Gains and losses up to the date of retirement belong to all old partners.

teach.ask: Gappu is retiring. Explain what happens to revaluation profit and reserves.

topics.title: Disposal of the amount due to a retiring partner

learn.hook: Cash now, a loan to be repaid, or instalments with interest? The firm's bank balance decides how the retiring partner is paid.
points: Paid in full immediately: Dr Retiring Partner's Capital A/c, Cr Cash/Bank A/c.
Not paid immediately: Dr Retiring Partner's Capital A/c, Cr Retiring Partner's Loan A/c. The loan appears on the liabilities side of the balance sheet.
Partly paid: cash for the part paid, loan for the balance.
Paid in instalments with interest: interest on the outstanding balance is credited to the loan account (Dr Interest A/c, Cr Loan A/c); each payment is debited to it (Dr Loan A/c, Cr Bank A/c).
Interest on the retiring partner's loan is an expense of the firm, charged to the Profit and Loss Account.

Dr Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c / Cr Cash A/c

topics.title: Adjusting continuing partners' capitals

learn.hook: One partner leaves with a big cheque. The rest may need to top up – or take some back – so their capitals match the new ratio.
points: After settling the retiring partner, continuing partners may agree to keep capitals in their new profit-sharing ratio.
If the total capital of the new firm is given, each partner's required capital = total × his new share.
If not given, the total of continuing partners' adjusted capitals (after all adjustments and payment to the retiring partner) is taken as the total capital.
Deficiency: partner brings cash (Dr Cash, Cr Capital). Surplus: partner withdraws (Dr Capital, Cr Cash) or it goes to current account.

example.q: After C's retirement, A and B (new ratio 3:2) agree that the firm's total capital will be ₹3,00,000. Their adjusted capitals are A ₹1,50,000 and B ₹1,40,000. Adjust.

learn.reallife: Partners of a Ludhiana hosiery firm often top up capital after a senior partner retires so the bank sees a well-funded, balanced firm.

games.title: Capital adjustment checks
items: A partner with a deficiency in capital brings cash into the firm.
Dr Cash, Cr his Capital.
If total capital is not specified, the continuing partners' combined adjusted capitals are taken as total.
That total is then split in the new ratio.

topics.title: Death of a partner: profit up to the date of death

learn.hook: A partner passes away mid-year. His family is entitled to his share of profit up to that day – but the year's accounts are not ready. How do we estimate it?
points: On death, accounting is like retirement: new ratio, gaining ratio, goodwill, revaluation and reserves are dealt with, and the amount due is paid to the executors.
Time basis: deceased's share = Previous year's (or average) profit × months up to death ÷ 12 × his share.
Turnover (sales) basis: estimated profit = Sales up to death × (last year's profit ÷ last year's sales); deceased's share = that × his share.
Entry: Dr Profit and Loss Suspense A/c, Cr Deceased Partner's Capital A/c (the profit is not yet ascertained, so a suspense account is used).

example.q: Accounts close on 31 March. D (share 1/4) dies on 30 June 2025. Last year's profit was ₹1,20,000. Find his share on time basis.
example.answer: ₹7,500, credited to D's capital by debiting Profit and Loss Suspense A/c.

learn.hook: The family of a deceased partner deserves a clear, fair statement. Two accounts – his capital account and the executor's account – provide it.

chapters.title: Part I: Dissolution of Partnership Firm

topics.title: Dissolution of partnership vs dissolution of firm

learn.hook: A partner retires and the shop stays open – or the shutters come down for good. Both are 'dissolution', but they are very different.
points: Dissolution of partnership: the existing agreement ends and a new one is formed (e.g. on admission, retirement, death or change in ratio); the firm continues.
Dissolution of firm: the partnership among ALL partners ends; business stops, assets are sold and liabilities paid, and the books are closed.
Dissolution of a firm always dissolves the partnership, but dissolution of partnership does not necessarily dissolve the firm.
Differences: continuation of business, court intervention (possible only for dissolution of firm), settlement of assets and liabilities, and closure of books.

example.q: Ravi, Sana and Joseph run a café. Joseph retires; Ravi and Sana carry on. Later the café closes and everything is sold. Classify each event.
steps: Joseph's retirement: agreement ends, business continues → dissolution of partnership.
Closing the café, selling assets and paying debts → dissolution of firm.
example.answer: Retirement = dissolution of partnership; closure = dissolution of firm.

learn.reallife: Many small partnership firms during the COVID-19 lockdowns in India had to choose between reconstituting with fewer partners and dissolving the firm entirely.

topics.title: Modes of dissolution of a firm

learn.hook: Firms can end by choice, by law, by circumstance, by a letter, or by a judge's order. Know all five doors out.
points: By agreement (Sec 40): with the consent of all partners, or as per a contract among them.
Compulsory dissolution (Sec 41): when all partners or all but one become insolvent, or the business becomes unlawful.
On certain contingencies (Sec 42), subject to contract: expiry of the fixed term, completion of the venture, death of a partner, or insolvency of a partner.
By notice (Sec 43): in a partnership at will, any partner may give written notice to all others of his intention to dissolve.

By court (Sec 44), on a partner's suit: unsound mind, permanent incapacity, misconduct affecting the business, persistent breach of agreement, transfer of whole interest to a third party, business can be carried on only at a loss, or just and equitable grounds.

example.q: Three partners formed a firm only to organise a trade fair in Pragati Maidan. The fair is over. What happens to the firm?
steps: The firm was formed for a particular venture.
On completion of the venture, the firm is dissolved on the happening of a contingency (unless the partners agree otherwise).
example.answer: It is dissolved on completion of the venture (Section 42).

learn.reallife: If a government ban makes a product illegal – as happened with some single-use plastics in India – a firm dealing only in it faces compulsory dissolution.

topics.title: Settlement of accounts: Section 48

learn.hook: When a firm closes, there's a strict queue for the money. Outsiders first, partners' loans next, capitals after that.
points: Losses, including deficiencies of capital, are paid first out of profits, then out of capital, and lastly by partners individually in their profit-sharing ratio.

Assets (including sums contributed by partners) are applied in this order: (i) debts of the firm to third parties; (ii) partners' loans/advances (as distinct from capital); (iii) partners' capitals; (iv) any surplus is shared in the profit-sharing ratio.
Private assets and liabilities (Sec 49): firm's property goes first to firm's debts; a partner's private property goes first to his private debts, and any surplus may be used for the firm's debts.
This course excludes piecemeal distribution, sale of the firm to a company and insolvency of partners.

example.q: On dissolution, a firm has ₹3,00,000 after selling assets. Creditors are owed ₹1,80,000 and partner A's loan is ₹40,000. Partners' capitals total ₹1,00,000. How is the cash used?
steps: Capitals of ₹1,00,000 can be paid only ₹80,000; the ₹20,000 shortfall is a loss shared in the profit-sharing ratio.
example.answer: Creditors → A's loan → capitals; ₹20,000 loss shared by partners in profit-sharing ratio.

learn.reallife: Like passengers stepping off an Indian Railways coach in order, claims are settled strictly: outside creditors, then partners' loans, then capitals.

topics.title: Realisation Account: transfers and sales

learn.hook: On dissolution, every asset is sold and every outside debt paid – all through one account that tells you if the firm sold at a profit or a loss.
points: Realisation Account is a nominal account prepared on dissolution to record the sale of assets and payment of liabilities and find the profit or loss on realisation.
Debit: all assets at book value EXCEPT cash/bank and fictitious assets (e.g. advertisement suspense, P&L debit balance). Entry: Dr Realisation A/c, Cr Asset A/cs.

Credit: all outside liabilities and provisions against assets (e.g. provision for doubtful debts, accumulated depreciation). Partners' loans and capitals and reserves are NOT transferred. Entry: Dr Liability A/cs, Cr Realisation A/c.
Sale of assets: Dr Cash/Bank, Cr Realisation. Payment of liabilities: Dr Realisation, Cr Cash/Bank.
If no realisable value is given, assume tangible assets realise their book value and intangible assets (like goodwill) realise nothing.

example.q: Balance sheet of A and B (1:1): Building ₹2,00,000; Machinery ₹1,00,000; Stock ₹50,000; Debtors ₹40,000 less provision ₹2,000; Cash ₹20,000. Creditors ₹60,000; Bills payable ₹20,000; A's loan ₹30,000; General reserve ₹28,000; Capitals A ₹1,50,000, B ₹1,20,000. Which items go to the Realisation Account at book value?
steps: Debit side: Building 2,00,000; Machinery 1,00,000; Stock 50,000; Debtors 40,000 = ₹3,90,000.
Credit side: Provision 2,000; Creditors 60,000; Bills payable 20,000 = ₹82,000.
Cash stays in the Cash Account; A's loan, General reserve and capitals are not transferred.
example.answer: Assets ₹3,90,000 debited; liabilities and provision ₹82,000 credited.

topics.title: Assets and liabilities taken over; creditors accepting assets

learn.hook: A partner wants to keep the delivery van; a supplier happily takes stock instead of cash. These twists change the entries, so watch carefully.
points: Asset taken over by a partner: Dr Partner's Capital A/c, Cr Realisation A/c (at the agreed value).

learn.hook: Closing down costs money – brokers, lawyers, transport. Who pays, and who finally bears it? Five cases, five different entries.
points: Expenses paid by the firm: Dr Realisation A/c, Cr Cash A/c.

To be borne by a partner and paid by him: no entry. Borne by a partner but paid by the firm: Dr Partner's Capital A/c, Cr Cash A/c.
A partner is given a fixed remuneration for completing the dissolution and bears the expenses: Dr Realisation A/c, Cr Partner's Capital A/c (remuneration); no entry for the actual expenses.
Balance of Realisation: profit → Dr Realisation, Cr Partners' Capital A/cs; loss → Dr Partners' Capital A/cs, Cr Realisation; both in the profit-sharing ratio.

topics.title: Closing the books: capitals, loans and cash

learn.hook: The final scene: every account must hit zero. If the cash account balances to the last rupee, you've done the dissolution right.
points: Accumulated profits and reserves are credited, and accumulated losses and fictitious assets debited, to partners' capitals in the profit-sharing ratio.
Partner's loan is paid after outside liabilities: Dr Partner's Loan A/c, Cr Cash A/c (it does not go through Realisation).
After the realisation profit/loss is transferred, each capital account is closed: credit balance paid (Dr Capital, Cr Cash); debit balance brought in by the partner (Dr Cash, Cr Capital).
The cash/bank account closes automatically when final payments are made – total receipts equal total payments.
Key journal entries: assets/liabilities to Realisation; sale and payments; reserve distribution; loss/profit transfer; partner's loan payment; final settlement of capitals.

example.q: Balance sheet of A and B (1:1): Building ₹2,00,000; Machinery ₹1,00,000; Stock ₹50,000; Debtors ₹40,000 less provision ₹2,000; Cash ₹20,000. Creditors ₹60,000; Bills payable ₹20,000; A's loan ₹30,000; General reserve ₹28,000; Capitals A ₹1,50,000, B ₹1,20,000. Assets realise ₹4,01,000; liabilities ₹80,000 and expenses ₹3,000 are paid; profit on realisation ₹10,000. Settle the partners.
steps: Total ₹3,08,000 = cash available. The cash account closes.

learn.reallife: Like the final settlement of a closed bank account, every balance must be paid out and the books closed with nothing left over.

chapters.title: Part II: Accounting for Share Capital

topics.title: Features of a company

learn.hook: Reliance, Infosys and Tata Steel outlive their founders and are owned by lakhs of shareholders who never meet. What makes such a creature possible?
points: A company is an artificial person created by law, with a separate legal entity distinct from its members – it can own property, sue and be sued in its own name.
Perpetual succession: members may come and go, but the company continues.
Limited liability: in a company limited by shares, a member's liability is limited to the unpaid amount on his shares.
Common seal: traditionally the company's official signature (now optional under the Companies Act, 2013). Shares of a public company are freely transferable.
Separation of ownership and management: shareholders own the company, but an elected Board of Directors manages it.

example.q: Priya holds 100 shares of ₹10 each in a company, on which ₹7 per share has been paid. The company goes into heavy debt. What is the most she can be asked to pay?
steps: Limited liability: only the unpaid amount on her shares can be claimed.
example.answer: ₹300 – her personal assets are otherwise safe.

learn.reallife: Lakhs of Indians hold shares of companies through demat accounts; they own a slice of the company, while professional boards and managers run it.

topics.title: Kinds of companies

learn.hook: Private, public, one-person, government, holding, subsidiary, associate – company labels can feel like a cricket team's batting order. Let's set the line-up.
points: By liability: company limited by shares (liability up to unpaid amount on shares), company limited by guarantee (liability up to the amount members undertake to contribute on winding up), unlimited company (no limit).

By membership: private company – minimum 2 and maximum 200 members (excluding employee/ex-employee members), restricts transfer of shares and cannot invite the public to subscribe; public company – minimum 7 members, no maximum; One Person Company – only one person as member.
Government company: at least 51% of paid-up share capital is held by the Central Government and/or State Government(s).
Holding and subsidiary: a holding company controls the composition of the subsidiary's Board of Directors or controls more than half of its total voting power.

Associate company: a company over which another has significant influence – control of at least 20% of total voting power or of business decisions under an agreement – but which is not its subsidiary.

example.q: The Government of India holds 60% of the paid-up share capital of a company. Classify it.
steps: The test for a government company is at least 51% of paid-up share capital held by government(s).

learn.reallife: Companies like Coal India and ONGC are government companies, while a solo founder's start-up may begin life as a One Person Company.

topics.title: Shares: preference and equity

learn.hook: Two shareholders, same company: one gets a fixed 8% dividend first, the other gets whatever is left – and the vote. Which would you choose?
points: A share is a unit of a company's share capital. Shares are movable property, transferable as provided in the articles.
Preference shares carry two preferential rights: dividend at a fixed rate before equity holders, and repayment of capital before equity holders on winding up.

Types: cumulative (unpaid dividend accumulates) vs non-cumulative; participating (share surplus profits) vs non-participating; convertible vs non-convertible into equity; redeemable vs irredeemable. Under the Companies Act, 2013, a company cannot issue irredeemable preference shares.
Equity shares are those that are not preference shares. They carry residual rights to profit and capital, normal voting rights, and a dividend that varies with profits.

example.q: A company has 10,000 8% cumulative preference shares of ₹100 each. It paid no dividend last year. This year it decides to pay preference dividend. How much is due?
steps: Cumulative: last year's unpaid ₹80,000 is carried forward.
Total due = ₹1,60,000 before any equity dividend.

topics.title: Categories of share capital

learn.hook: A company may be allowed ₹5 lakh of capital, offer ₹4 lakh, get applications for ₹3.6 lakh and collect even less. Each layer has its own name.
points: Authorised (registered or nominal) capital: the maximum capital a company is allowed to raise, stated in its Memorandum.
Issued capital: the part of authorised capital offered for subscription (including shares issued to vendors). Unissued capital: the rest.
Subscribed capital: the part of issued capital actually taken up. It may be 'subscribed and fully paid up' or 'subscribed but not fully paid up'.
Called-up capital: the amount on subscribed shares that the company has asked shareholders to pay; uncalled capital is the rest. Paid-up capital = called-up capital − calls in arrears.
Reserve capital: a portion of uncalled capital that the company, by special resolution, decides to call only on winding up.

example.q: Authorised: 50,000 shares of ₹10. Issued: 40,000. Subscribed: 36,000. ₹8 per share called; holders of 1,000 shares have not paid the last ₹2 call. Find each category.

topics.title: Share capital in the balance sheet and notes

learn.hook: Open any listed company's annual report: 'Share capital – Note 2'. Behind that one line sits a whole table. Let's read it like a pro.
points: Balance sheet (Schedule III): Equity and Liabilities → Shareholders' Funds → Share Capital, with details in Notes to Accounts.
Note on Share Capital shows: Authorised capital; Issued capital; Subscribed capital – (a) Subscribed and fully paid up, (b) Subscribed but not fully paid up (called-up less calls in arrears).
Amount in the balance sheet = subscribed and fully paid up + (subscribed but not fully paid up − calls in arrears) + share forfeiture account balance.
Calls in advance are not part of share capital; they are shown under Other Current Liabilities.
Securities premium is shown under Reserves and Surplus, not under Share Capital.

example.q: A company issued 40,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, fully called. All were subscribed. Calls in arrears are ₹5,000. Show share capital.

learn.reallife: The Companies Act, 2013 requires every Indian company to present its balance sheet in the Schedule III format, so investors everywhere see the same layout.

topics.title: Issue of shares at par: process and entries

learn.hook: An IPO opens: you apply with some money, get an allotment message, then pay calls. Each step is a journal entry in the company's books.
points: Process: issue of prospectus → receipt of applications → allotment → calls. The company must receive minimum subscription of 90% of the issue before allotting shares.
Shares may be issued for cash in a lump sum or in instalments (application, allotment, first call, final call). Issue at par means at face value.

Entries: Bank Dr / Share Application Cr; Share Application Dr / Share Capital Cr; Share Allotment Dr / Share Capital Cr; Bank Dr / Share Allotment Cr; Share First Call Dr / Share Capital Cr; Bank Dr / Share First Call Cr.
Without separate call accounts, money received on allotment and calls can be credited directly to Share Capital (Bank Dr / Share Capital Cr).

example.q: Mehta Ltd issues 10,000 equity shares of ₹10 at par: ₹3 on application, ₹4 on allotment, ₹3 on first and final call. All money is received. Find amounts at each stage.
steps: Application: 10,000 × 3 = ₹30,000 (Bank Dr / Share Application Cr; then transferred to Share Capital).
Allotment: 10,000 × 4 = ₹40,000 (Share Allotment Dr / Share Capital Cr; Bank Dr / Share Allotment Cr).

topics.title: Issue of shares at a premium; discount rule

learn.hook: Investors happily pay ₹12 for a ₹10 share of a strong company. That extra ₹2 can't be spent on anything you like – the law tells you where it may go.
points: Issue at premium: issue price above face value. The premium is credited to Securities Premium Account (Reserves and Surplus), usually collected with allotment.
Allotment with premium: Share Allotment A/c Dr (total) / Share Capital A/c Cr (capital part), Securities Premium A/c Cr (premium part).

Section 52 uses of securities premium: issuing fully paid bonus shares; writing off preliminary expenses; writing off expenses of, or commission paid or discount allowed on, any issue of shares or debentures; providing premium payable on redemption of preference shares or debentures; buy-back of own shares (Section 68).
Securities premium cannot be used to pay dividend.
Section 53: a company cannot issue shares at a discount; such issue is void. Exception: sweat equity shares (Section 54).

example.q: 10,000 shares of ₹10 issued at ₹12: ₹3 on application, ₹5 on allotment (including premium), ₹4 on first and final call. Show the allotment entry.
steps: Share Allotment Dr 50,000 / Share Capital Cr 30,000, Securities Premium Cr 20,000.
example.answer: Dr Share Allotment ₹50,000 / Cr Share Capital ₹30,000, Cr Securities Premium ₹20,000

learn.reallife: Hot IPOs on Dalal Street are priced well above the ₹10 or ₹1 face value; the difference sits in securities premium in the company's books.

topics.title: Calls in arrears and calls in advance

learn.hook: Some shareholders pay late; a few eager ones pay early. The company tracks both in separate accounts.
points: Calls in arrears: amount called but not paid by some shareholders. Entry when receiving a call: Bank A/c Dr (amount received), Calls in Arrears A/c Dr (unpaid) / Share Call A/c Cr.
Calls in arrears are deducted from called-up capital in the Share Capital note.
Calls in advance: money received before a call is made. Entry: Bank A/c Dr / Calls in Advance A/c Cr.
When the call is later made: Calls in Advance A/c Dr / Share Call A/c Cr.
Calls in advance appear under Other Current Liabilities until adjusted. (Interest on these is outside this course.)

example.q: First call of ₹3 on 10,000 shares is made. Holders of 1,000 shares fail to pay. Record the receipt.
steps: Bank Dr 27,000; Calls in Arrears Dr 3,000 / Share First Call Cr 30,000.

topics.title: Under-subscription, over-subscription and pro-rata allotment

learn.hook: A hot IPO is subscribed 30 times; a dull one limps to 92%. Each needs different handling of application money.
points: Under-subscription: applications are fewer than shares offered. If at least the minimum subscription (90%) is received, shares are allotted to all applicants.
Over-subscription: applications exceed shares offered. The company may (a) reject some applications and refund money, (b) allot pro-rata, or (c) combine both.

Pro-rata allotment: shares allotted in proportion to shares applied. Excess application money of pro-rata applicants is adjusted towards allotment (and calls, if the articles allow); any balance is refunded.
Entries: Share Application Dr / Share Capital Cr (allotted), Share Allotment Cr (excess adjusted), Bank Cr (refund).

example.q: A company offers 10,000 shares of ₹10: ₹3 on application, ₹4 on allotment, ₹3 on call. It receives applications for 15,000 shares and allots pro-rata. Find cash due on allotment.

topics.title: Shares issued for consideration other than cash

learn.hook: A company buys a factory but pays in shares instead of cash. How many shares does the seller get?
points: A company may issue shares to vendors for assets or a business purchased. Entry 1: Assets A/c Dr / Vendor A/c Cr (purchase consideration).
Entry 2: Vendor A/c Dr / Share Capital A/c Cr (and Securities Premium A/c Cr if issued at a premium).
Number of shares = Purchase consideration ÷ Issue price per share.
When a business is bought: Assets Dr, Goodwill Dr (if consideration exceeds net assets) / Liabilities Cr, Vendor Cr, Capital Reserve Cr (if consideration is less than net assets).
Shares may also be issued to promoters for their services in forming the company; Share Capital is credited and the cost of their services is treated as part of formation (incorporation) costs.

example.q: A company buys machinery for ₹4,40,000 and pays by issuing equity shares of ₹10 at a premium of 10%. Find the number of shares and the entry.

topics.title: Private placement, ESOP and sweat equity

learn.hook: Not every share issue is a public IPO. Some go to a chosen few investors, some reward employees, and some pay for brains instead of cash.
points: Private placement (Section 42): offer of securities to a select group of persons (not the public) through a private placement offer letter. Under the rules, an offer may be made to at most 200 persons in a financial year, excluding qualified institutional buyers and employees under ESOP.

Employee Stock Option Plan, ESOP (Section 2(37)): an option given to directors, officers or employees of the company (or its holding/subsidiary) to buy or subscribe for shares at a future date at a predetermined price.
An option is a right, not an obligation; the employee decides whether to exercise it.

Sweat equity shares (Section 2(88)): shares issued by a company to its directors or employees at a discount or for consideration other than cash, for providing know-how, intellectual property rights or value additions. This is the only case where shares may be issued at a discount (Sections 53 and 54).

example.q: An employee holds ESOP options for 1,000 shares at an exercise price of ₹50 each. He exercises all of them. How much does the company receive?
steps: He pays the predetermined price for each share.

learn.reallife: Indian start-ups widely use ESOPs to attract talent – employees join on lower salaries hoping their options will be valuable after a funding round or IPO.
