topics.title: Forfeiture of shares

learn.hook: Miss your calls repeatedly and the company can take your shares away – keeping what you already paid. That's forfeiture.
points: Forfeiture: cancellation of shares for non-payment of allotment or calls, after due notice, as per the articles. Money already received is not refunded.
Shares at par: Share Capital Dr (called-up amount) / Unpaid Allotment or Calls Cr / Share Forfeiture Cr (amount received).
Shares at premium, premium RECEIVED: Securities Premium is not touched; debit Share Capital with called-up amount.
Shares at premium, premium NOT received: also debit Securities Premium with the unpaid premium.
Pro-rata cases: excess application money already adjusted counts as received; find unpaid amounts carefully. Share Forfeiture balance is added to paid-up capital in the Share Capital note.

example.q: Raj holds 100 shares of ₹10 issued at par. He paid ₹3 on application and ₹4 on allotment but not the ₹3 final call. The shares are forfeited. Pass the entry.
steps: Unpaid call: 100 × 3 = ₹300 → credit Share Final Call.
example.answer: Share Capital Dr ₹1,000 / Share Final Call Cr ₹300, Share Forfeiture Cr ₹700

topics.title: Re-issue of forfeited shares

learn.hook: Forfeited shares are back with the company. It can sell them again – even cheaply – but only so cheaply.
points: Forfeited shares may be re-issued at par, at a premium or at a discount. The discount on re-issue cannot exceed the amount forfeited on those shares.
Entry: Bank Dr (amount received), Share Forfeiture Dr (discount allowed) / Share Capital Cr (paid-up value credited); premium, if any, to Securities Premium Cr.
After re-issue, the remaining forfeited amount on re-issued shares is a capital profit: Share Forfeiture Dr / Capital Reserve Cr.
If only some forfeited shares are re-issued, transfer to capital reserve only the gain on those shares: (forfeited amount per share × shares re-issued) − discount allowed.
Balance sheet: capital reserve goes to Reserves and Surplus; any forfeiture balance on shares not re-issued stays in the Share Capital note.

example.q: 100 forfeited shares (₹10 each; ₹700 forfeited) are re-issued at ₹8 per share fully paid. Pass entries.
steps: Bank Dr 800; Share Forfeiture Dr 200 / Share Capital Cr 1,000.

topics.title: Debentures: meaning and comparison with shares

learn.hook: When NHAI or a big company raises money through bonds, investors become lenders, not owners. That loan certificate is a debenture.
points: A debenture is a written acknowledgement of a debt by a company under its common seal (where used), carrying a fixed rate of interest and repayable as per terms.
A debenture trust deed appoints trustees to protect debenture-holders' interests and records terms like interest, security and redemption.
Debentures and bonds are borrowed (debt) capital; debenture-holders are creditors of the company.

Shares vs debentures: shareholders are owners, get dividend (an appropriation, paid only from profits) and have voting rights; debenture-holders are creditors, get interest (a charge, payable even in a loss), have no voting rights, may be secured, and are repaid before shareholders on winding up.
Debentures may be issued at a discount; shares cannot (except sweat equity). Debentures may be convertible into shares.

example.q: Neha buys 50 9% debentures of ₹100 each. The company makes a loss this year. Does she get interest? How much?
steps: Interest on debentures is a charge, payable whether there is profit or loss.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways' financing arm IRFC and many PSUs raise thousands of crores through bonds that work just like debentures.

topics.title: Types of debentures

learn.hook: Secured or naked, perpetual or redeemable, convertible or not, zero coupon or not, registered or bearer – debentures come in many flavours.
points: Security: secured debentures carry a charge on assets; unsecured (naked) debentures have no such charge.
Tenure: redeemable debentures are repaid after a fixed period; perpetual (irredeemable) debentures are not repayable during the life of the company.
Convertibility: fully convertible (wholly into shares), partly convertible, and non-convertible debentures (NCDs).
Coupon rate: specific coupon rate debentures carry a stated interest rate; zero coupon rate debentures carry no interest but are issued at a deep discount and redeemed at face value.
Registration: registered debentures – holders' names recorded and transfer needs a transfer deed; bearer debentures – transferable by mere delivery, interest paid to whoever holds the coupon.

example.q: A company issues debentures of face value ₹1,000 at ₹750, with no interest, redeemable at ₹1,000 after 5 years. What type is it, and what does the investor earn?
steps: No interest → zero coupon rate debenture.
example.answer: Zero coupon debenture; return ₹250 per debenture.

learn.reallife: Indian investors buy NCDs from NBFCs for steady interest, while many PSU bonds are secured and redeemable after a fixed tenure.

topics.title: Issue of debentures for cash at par, premium or discount

learn.hook: Like shares, debentures can be issued in one go or in instalments – and unlike shares, they may be issued at a discount.
points: Lump sum / instalments: Bank Dr / Debenture Application & Allotment Cr; then Debenture Application & Allotment Dr / Debentures Cr. Calls are recorded like share calls.
At premium: Debenture Application & Allotment Dr (issue price) / Debentures Cr (face value), Securities Premium Cr (premium).
At discount: Debenture Application & Allotment Dr (issue price), Discount on Issue of Debentures Dr (discount) / Debentures Cr (face value).
Securities premium on debentures can be used as per Section 52, e.g. to write off discount or loss on issue of debentures.
Over-subscription: excess application money is refunded (Debenture Application & Allotment Dr / Bank Cr) or adjusted towards allotment.

example.q: A company issues 5,000 9% debentures of ₹100 each at a discount of 10%, payable fully on application. Pass the entries.
steps: Cash received = 5,000 × 90 = ₹4,50,000: Bank Dr / Debenture Application & Allotment Cr.
Debenture Application & Allotment Dr 4,50,000, Discount on Issue of Debentures Dr 50,000 / 9% Debentures Cr 5,00,000.

learn.hook: A bank lends ₹10 lakh but wants extra comfort. The company hands over its own debentures as a backup pledge – collateral security.
points: Collateral security is a subsidiary or additional security given besides the primary security for a loan. The lender can sell the debentures only if the borrower defaults.
No interest is paid on debentures issued as collateral (interest is paid only on the actual loan).
First method: no journal entry; the fact is shown in a note under the loan in Long-term Borrowings.
Second method: Debenture Suspense A/c Dr / Debentures A/c Cr (face value). In the balance sheet, debentures are shown under Long-term Borrowings and Debenture Suspense is deducted from them.
When the loan is repaid, the debentures are cancelled (reverse entry under the second method).

Balance sheet note: 9% Debentures 12,00,000 less Debenture Suspense 12,00,000 = nil; Bank Loan 10,00,000 (secured by collateral debentures).

topics.title: Terms of issue and redemption of debentures

learn.hook: Issue at par, premium or discount; redeem at par or at a premium – six combinations, one rule: put any loss in a 'loss on issue' account up front.
points: Six cases: issued at par/premium/discount × redeemable at par/premium.
If redeemable at a premium, record the premium payable on redemption as a liability (Premium on Redemption of Debentures A/c Cr) at the time of issue, and debit Loss on Issue of Debentures A/c.
Issue at discount, redeemable at premium: Loss on Issue = discount + premium on redemption.
Issue at premium, redeemable at premium: Securities Premium Cr (issue premium) and Premium on Redemption Cr; Loss on Issue Dr = redemption premium.
Actual redemption of debentures (methods, DRR, sinking fund) is outside the CBSE syllabus for this course.

example.q: 1,000 debentures of ₹100 are issued at a 5% discount and redeemable at a 10% premium. Pass the issue entry (cash received in full).

Debentures Cr 1,00,000; Premium on Redemption of Debentures Cr 10,000.

topics.title: Interest on debentures

learn.hook: Debenture interest is the rent a company pays for borrowed money – on the face value, at the coupon rate, often twice a year.
points: Interest is calculated on the FACE (nominal) value at the coupon rate, regardless of issue price.
Many companies pay interest half-yearly: half-yearly interest = face value × rate × 6/12.

Entries: Debenture Interest A/c Dr / Debentureholders' A/c Cr (interest due); Debentureholders' A/c Dr / Bank A/c Cr (payment); Statement of Profit and Loss Dr / Debenture Interest A/c Cr (transfer at year-end).
Debenture interest is a finance cost and a charge against profit. (TDS on debenture interest is excluded from this course.)
If debentures were issued during the year, interest is only for the months they were outstanding.

example.q: A company has ₹5,00,000 10% debentures, interest payable half-yearly. Find each half-year's interest and the year's total.
steps: Year's total = ₹50,000, transferred to the Statement of Profit and Loss.

topics.title: Writing off discount or loss on issue of debentures

learn.hook: A discount on issue is a cost of borrowing. Don't carry it around for years – write it off in the year of allotment.
points: Discount or loss on issue of debentures is written off in the year the debentures are allotted.
Order: first from Securities Premium (if any balance exists), then the balance from the Statement of Profit and Loss as a finance cost.
Entry: Securities Premium A/c Dr, Statement of Profit and Loss Dr / Discount (or Loss) on Issue of Debentures A/c Cr.
Using securities premium for this purpose is allowed by Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013.

example.q: Loss on issue of debentures is ₹60,000. Securities Premium has a balance of ₹40,000. Write off the loss.
steps: Balance ₹20,000 from Statement of Profit and Loss.
Securities Premium Dr 40,000; Statement of P&L Dr 20,000 / Loss on Issue of Debentures Cr 60,000.

chapters.title: Part II: Financial Statements of a Company

topics.title: Financial statements: meaning, nature and objectives

learn.hook: Every year, Infosys, Tata Motors and your neighbourhood listed company publish a thick annual report. Its heart is a few pages of financial statements.
points: Financial statements are the end products of the accounting process. For a company they include the Balance Sheet, the Statement of Profit and Loss, Notes to Accounts and the Cash Flow Statement (Section 2(40)).

Nature: they are based on recorded facts, accounting conventions (e.g. conservatism, consistency), postulates (e.g. going concern, money measurement) and personal judgements (e.g. depreciation method, inventory valuation).
Objectives: provide information about economic resources and obligations, about earning capacity (profitability), about cash flows, and to judge management's effectiveness (stewardship).
They are general-purpose statements used by many groups – investors, lenders, creditors, government and employees.

example.q: A company values inventory at cost or market price, whichever is lower, and charges depreciation by the straight-line method. Which elements of 'nature' are at work?
steps: Lower of cost or market reflects the convention of conservatism.
Choosing straight-line depreciation is a personal judgement.
Both rest on recorded facts (purchase cost of assets and stock).
example.answer: Accounting conventions and personal judgements applied to recorded facts.

topics.title: Schedule III balance sheet and shareholders' funds

learn.hook: One format for every company in India – from a small private company to Reliance. Learn it once, read every balance sheet.
points: Section 129 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires financial statements to give a true and fair view, comply with accounting standards and follow the form in Schedule III.

Balance sheet has two parts: Equity and Liabilities (Shareholders' Funds; Share Application Money Pending Allotment; Non-current Liabilities; Current Liabilities) and Assets (Non-current Assets; Current Assets).
Shareholders' Funds: (a) Share Capital, (b) Reserves and Surplus, (c) Money received against Share Warrants.
Reserves and Surplus include capital reserve, securities premium, general reserve and surplus (balance in Statement of Profit and Loss); a debit balance of P&L is shown as a negative figure here.
Share Application Money Pending Allotment is shown as a separate head between Shareholders' Funds and Non-current Liabilities.

topics.title: Non-current and current liabilities

learn.hook: A 10-year debenture and next week's supplier bill are both liabilities – but they sit in very different places on the balance sheet.
points: Non-current Liabilities: (a) Long-term Borrowings – debentures, bonds, term loans from banks, public deposits; (b) Deferred Tax Liabilities (net); (c) Other Long-term Liabilities; (d) Long-term Provisions – e.g. provision for employee benefits like gratuity.

Current Liabilities: (a) Short-term Borrowings – bank overdraft, cash credit, loans repayable on demand; (b) Trade Payables – creditors and bills payable; (c) Other Current Liabilities; (d) Short-term Provisions – e.g. provision for tax.
Other Current Liabilities include calls in advance, unpaid dividend, interest accrued on borrowings, income received in advance and outstanding expenses.
A liability is current if it is due within 12 months after the reporting date or within the operating cycle, or is held for trading.

example.q: Classify: 9% Debentures; Bank overdraft; Bills payable; Provision for tax; Unpaid dividend; Provision for gratuity (long-term).
steps: Provision for tax → Short-term Provisions; Unpaid dividend → Other Current Liabilities; Gratuity → Long-term Provisions.

topics.title: Non-current and current assets

learn.hook: Factories, patents and long-term investments versus stock, debtors and cash – the assets side tells you how the company uses its money.
points: Non-current Assets: (a) Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets – (i) Property, Plant and Equipment (tangible: land, building, plant, furniture, vehicles), (ii) Intangible Assets (goodwill, patents, trademarks, copyrights, software), (iii) Capital Work-in-Progress (e.g. building under construction), (iv) Intangible Assets under Development.
Also non-current: (b) Non-current Investments, (c) Deferred Tax Assets (net), (d) Long-term Loans and Advances (e.g. capital advances, security deposits), (e) Other Non-current Assets.

Current Assets: (a) Current Investments, (b) Inventories (raw materials, work-in-progress, finished goods, stock-in-trade, stores and spares, loose tools), (c) Trade Receivables (debtors and bills receivable), (d) Cash and Cash Equivalents (cash, bank balances, cheques and drafts on hand), (e) Short-term Loans and Advances, (f) Other Current Assets (e.g. accrued income).
Provision for doubtful debts is deducted from trade receivables, and accumulated depreciation from PPE.

steps: Building under construction → Capital Work-in-Progress; Cheques in hand → Cash and Cash Equivalents; long-held investments → Non-current Investments.

topics.title: Operating cycle, notes to accounts and classifying items

learn.hook: A bakery's cycle is a day; a shipyard's is years. The operating cycle decides what counts as 'current'.
points: Operating cycle: time between acquisition of assets for processing and their realisation in cash or cash equivalents. If it cannot be identified, it is assumed to be 12 months.

An asset is current if it is expected to be realised, sold or consumed in the normal operating cycle; is held mainly for trading; is expected to be realised within 12 months after the reporting date; or is cash/cash equivalent not restricted for more than 12 months. All others are non-current.
A liability is current if it is expected to be settled in the normal operating cycle, is held mainly for trading, or is due within 12 months after the reporting date.

Notes to Accounts give details behind each balance sheet and P&L line (e.g. breakup of share capital, reserves, PPE), accounting policies and contingent liabilities – keeping the main statements short.
Exercise type: classify a given item under the correct major head and sub-head of Schedule III.

example.q: A rice mill ages its premium basmati rice for 2 years before selling it, as is normal in that trade. Is this stock current or non-current?
steps: Its normal operating cycle includes the ageing period.

topics.title: Statement of Profit and Loss (Schedule III)

learn.hook: Revenue in, expenses out, profit before tax, tax, profit for the period – the Statement of Profit and Loss tells the year's story in one column.
points: Revenue from operations (sale of products, sale of services, other operating revenues such as scrap sales) + Other income (interest, dividend, profit on sale of assets/investments) = Total income.

topics.title: Uses and limitations of financial statements

chapters.title: Part II: Analysis of Financial Statements

topics.title: Analysis of financial statements: meaning, significance and objectives

learn.hook: A balance sheet is a photo; analysis is the X-ray. It shows what the numbers really mean for profit and safety.
points: Analysis of financial statements is the systematic study of relationships among items in the financial statements to judge profitability and financial position.
Analysis breaks data into meaningful groups and relationships; interpretation explains what those results mean. Analysis comes first, interpretation follows.

Users: finance manager (planning), top management (efficiency), trade payables (short-term solvency), lenders (long-term solvency and interest-paying ability), investors (profitability and growth), labour unions (capacity to pay wages), and government/analysts.
Objectives: assess earning capacity, managerial efficiency, short-term and long-term solvency, make inter-firm and intra-firm comparisons, and help forecasting and budgeting.

learn.hook: A doctor has a stethoscope, BP cuff and blood test. An analyst has four tools too – and like all tools, they have limits.
points: Tools: comparative statements, common-size statements, ratio analysis and cash flow analysis (trend analysis is also used).

Vertical analysis studies relationships among items of one period (e.g. common-size statements); it is also called static analysis.

topics.title: Comparative statements

learn.hook: Revenue grew from ₹10 lakh to ₹12.5 lakh. Good – but did expenses grow faster? Comparative statements answer in two columns: absolute change and % change.
points: A comparative statement shows figures for two (or more) years side by side, with absolute change and percentage change.
Absolute change = Current year − Previous year. Percentage change = Absolute change ÷ Previous year × 100.
Comparative balance sheet compares items of equity, liabilities and assets; comparative statement of profit and loss compares revenue, expenses and profit.
Interpretation: e.g. if revenue grows faster than expenses, profit margins improve; if current liabilities rise faster than current assets, liquidity weakens.

topics.title: Accounting ratios: meaning, objectives, advantages and limitations

learn.hook: ₹50 lakh profit – good or bad? It depends on whether sales were ₹1 crore or ₹100 crore. Ratios turn raw numbers into meaning.
points: An accounting ratio is an arithmetical relationship between two related accounting figures. It may be expressed as a pure ratio (2:1), a percentage (25%), times (6 times) or a fraction.
Objectives: know the operational efficiency, liquidity, solvency and profitability of the business, and make inter-firm and intra-firm comparisons.
Advantages: helps judge efficiency of decisions, simplifies complex figures, helps comparative analysis, identifies problem areas, helps in SWOT analysis, and aids planning and forecasting.

Limitations: depends on the limitations of accounting data; ignores price-level changes and qualitative factors; may be affected by window dressing; different accounting policies reduce comparability; there is no universally accepted standard ratio.

topics.title: Types of ratios and liquidity ratios

learn.hook: Can the company pay its bills next month? Two quick ratios answer that – the current ratio and the quick ratio.
points: Traditional classification: Statement of Profit and Loss ratios (e.g. gross profit ratio), Balance Sheet ratios (e.g. current ratio, debt-equity), and Composite ratios using both (e.g. trade receivables turnover, return on investment).
Functional classification: liquidity, solvency, activity (turnover) and profitability ratios.
Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities. A ratio of 2:1 is traditionally considered safe.
Quick (liquid) ratio = Quick assets ÷ Current liabilities, where Quick assets = Current assets − Inventories − Prepaid expenses. 1:1 is considered ideal.
Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities. If CR = r and WC is known: CL = WC ÷ (r − 1), CA = CL × r.

example.q: Inventories ₹1,00,000; trade receivables ₹1,20,000; cash ₹60,000; prepaid expenses ₹20,000; current liabilities ₹1,50,000. Find current and quick ratios.

topics.title: Debt-equity and debt to capital employed

learn.hook: How much of the company is funded by lenders versus owners? Too much debt, and a bad year can sink it.
points: Debt-equity ratio = Long-term debts ÷ Shareholders' funds (equity). Long-term debts = Long-term borrowings + Long-term provisions.
Shareholders' funds = Share capital + Reserves and surplus (+ money received against share warrants). Alternatively: Non-current assets + Working capital − Non-current liabilities.
A lower debt-equity ratio means more security for lenders; a common safe norm is 2 : 1.
Debt to capital employed ratio = Long-term debts ÷ Capital employed, where Capital employed = Long-term debts + Shareholders' funds (or Non-current assets + Working capital).

topics.title: Gross profit ratio, operating ratio and operating profit ratio

learn.hook: Out of every ₹100 of sales, how much is left after the cost of goods – and after running the business? These three ratios tell you.

Operating profit ratio = Operating profit ÷ Net revenue from operations × 100, where operating profit = revenue − operating cost.
Operating profit ratio = 100 − Operating ratio.
Non-operating items (interest on investments, loss by fire, profit on sale of assets) are excluded from operating ratios.

topics.title: Ratio applications: effects of transactions and missing figures

learn.hook: Board-exam favourite: 'Will paying a creditor raise or lower the current ratio?' Master the logic, not just the formula.
points: When current ratio > 1: an equal decrease in CA and CL (e.g. paying a creditor) INCREASES the ratio; an equal increase (e.g. buying goods on credit) DECREASES it.
Transactions within current assets (e.g. collecting from debtors) do not change the current ratio; a current asset used for a non-current asset (buying machinery for cash) reduces it.
Debt-equity: issue of equity shares or conversion of debentures into shares reduces it; issue of debentures for cash increases it.
Missing figures: use the ratio definitions as equations, e.g. CR 2.5, QR 1.5, CL ₹80,000 → CA ₹2,00,000, quick assets ₹1,20,000, inventory ₹80,000 (if no prepaid expenses).
Comprehensive questions: compute several ratios from one set of statements – always identify CA, CL, equity, long-term debt and capital employed first.

topics.title: Cash flow statement: meaning, objectives and benefits

learn.hook: A company can report a big profit and still run out of cash to pay salaries. The cash flow statement shows where the money actually came from and went.
points: A cash flow statement shows inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period, classified into operating, investing and financing activities. It is prepared as per AS 3 (Revised).
Objective: to show the sources and uses of cash and cash equivalents, and to explain the change between the opening and closing balances.

Benefits: assess liquidity and the ability to generate cash; help short-term planning; allow comparison across firms (removes effects of different accounting treatments); evaluate changes in net assets and financial structure.
A cash inflow increases, and an outflow decreases, total cash and cash equivalents.
Movements WITHIN cash and cash equivalents (e.g. cash deposited into bank, or cash used to buy a 2-month treasury bill) are not cash flows.

example.q: Which of these is a cash flow? (a) ₹50,000 cash deposited into the bank; (b) machinery bought for ₹2,00,000 cash.
steps: (a) Cash moves to bank – both are cash and cash equivalents, so total is unchanged → not a cash flow.
(b) Cash leaves for a non-cash asset → a cash outflow (investing activity).

topics.title: Cash and cash equivalents

learn.hook: Cash is obvious. But a 60-day treasury bill? An overdraft? Knowing what counts as 'cash' is half the battle.
points: Cash comprises cash in hand and demand deposits with banks.

Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into known amounts of cash with insignificant risk of change in value – generally with maturity of three months or less from the date of acquisition (e.g. treasury bills, commercial paper).
In CBSE questions, current investments are treated as marketable securities and hence as cash equivalents.
Bank overdraft and cash credit are treated as short-term borrowings, and changes in them are shown under financing activities.
Equity shares are not cash equivalents because their value can change significantly.

topics.title: Operating, investing and financing activities

learn.hook: Every rupee in or out of a company falls into one of three buckets. Sort them right and the statement writes itself.
points: Operating activities: principal revenue-producing activities – cash from sale of goods and services, royalties, fees and commissions; cash paid to suppliers and employees; income tax paid (unless linked to investing/financing).

Investing activities: acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and investments – purchase/sale of fixed assets and intangibles, purchase/sale of shares or debentures of other companies (not held for trading), loans to others and their recovery.

Financing activities: changes in the size and composition of owners' capital and borrowings – issue of shares and debentures, long-term and short-term borrowings and their repayment, redemption, buy-back.
Exam type: classify given items into the three activities (for a non-financial company unless stated).

topics.title: Interest, dividend and income tax in the cash flow statement

learn.hook: Interest paid by a bank is part of its business; interest paid by a car-maker is a financing cost. Same item, different bucket.
points: Financial enterprise (e.g. a bank, NBFC): interest paid, interest received and dividends received are operating activities; dividends paid are financing.
Non-financial enterprise: interest paid and dividends paid are financing activities; interest received and dividends received are investing activities.
Dividends paid are always a financing activity.
Income tax paid is classified as an operating activity, unless it can be specifically identified with investing or financing activities. A tax refund received is an operating inflow.

example.q: Classify for (i) a bank and (ii) a cement company: interest received ₹50,000; dividend paid ₹30,000.
steps: Bank: interest received → operating; dividend paid → financing.
Cement company: interest received → investing; dividend paid → financing.

topics.title: Indirect method: from net profit to operating profit before working capital changes

learn.hook: Start with the profit figure, then undo everything that isn't cash or isn't operating. That's the indirect method – the only method in the CBSE syllabus.
points: Step 1 – Net profit before tax and extraordinary items: Change in surplus (closing − opening balance of Statement of P&L) + transfer to reserves + provision for tax made during the year + interim dividend + dividend of the previous year paid this year (under AS 4 revised, proposed dividend is not a liability).
Step 2 – Add non-cash and non-operating charges: depreciation, amortisation (goodwill, patents), loss on sale of fixed assets/investments, interest paid on borrowings/debentures (finance cost).
Step 3 – Deduct non-operating incomes: profit on sale of fixed assets/investments, interest received, dividends received.
The result is Operating Profit before Working Capital Changes.

example.q: Surplus rose from ₹50,000 to ₹1,30,000. Transfer to general reserve ₹20,000; provision for tax made ₹40,000; interim dividend ₹10,000. topics.title: Working capital changes and income tax paid

learn.hook: Profit is ready – but cash got stuck in extra stock and slow debtors. Working capital adjustments reveal the real operating cash.
points: Increase in a current asset (inventories, trade receivables, prepaid expenses) → DEDUCT; decrease → ADD.
Increase in a current liability (trade payables, outstanding expenses, income received in advance) → ADD; decrease → DEDUCT.
Exclude cash and cash equivalents (including current investments), short-term borrowings (financing) and provision for tax/dividend items from these adjustments.
Cash generated from operations = Operating profit before WC changes ± WC changes.
Net cash from operating activities = Cash generated from operations − Income tax paid.

topics.title: Investing and financing cash flows with working accounts

learn.hook: The balance sheet shows machinery up by ₹1 lakh. But how much was actually bought, and how much sold? Working accounts dig out hidden figures.
points: Machinery (fixed asset) account: Opening + Purchases = Depreciation (if charged to asset) + Book value of asset sold + Closing. Solve for the missing purchase.
Provision for depreciation account: Opening + Depreciation charged = Accumulated depreciation on asset sold + Closing.
Provision for tax account: Opening + Provision made = Tax paid + Closing. So tax paid = Opening + Provision made − Closing.
Investing: purchase (outflow) and sale proceeds (inflow) of fixed assets and investments; interest and dividend received (non-financial).
Financing: issue of shares/debentures (including premium) and borrowings (inflows); redemption, repayment, interest paid and dividends paid (outflows).

topics.title: Preparing the cash flow statement (AS 3 format)

learn.hook: Put the three blocks together, add them up, and the result must match the change in cash. If it does – you've nailed it.
points: Format (AS 3, indirect method): A. Cash Flows from Operating Activities; B. Cash Flows from Investing Activities; C. Cash Flows from Financing Activities.
Net increase/(decrease) in cash and cash equivalents = A + B + C.
Reconciliation: Opening cash and cash equivalents + Net increase (or − net decrease) = Closing cash and cash equivalents.
For a full question: compare two balance sheets, read additional information, prepare working accounts, then build A, B and C.
The direct method of computing operating cash flow is outside the CBSE syllabus.

example.q: Net cash from operating activities ₹1,60,000; investing ₹(1,55,000); financing ₹75,000. Opening cash and cash equivalents ₹40,000. Find the net change and closing balance.
steps: Check: this must equal the closing cash and cash equivalents in the balance sheet.
